title: CEO Interview with Charlie Cheng of CEO of TeRAM - Semiwiki
gist: TeRAM, a Silicon Valley startup spun out of Kilopass in 2018 and seed-funded with $37M in 2026, is building custom 3D SRAM memory chips designed to break the AI 'Memory Wall' by offering a per-compute-chip-customized memory business model similar to Broadcom's ASIC business, positioning itself as a bridge solution while the industry waits for true 3D DRAM bit-cell mass production.

themes.theme: TeRAM's Bet on 3D SRAM to Break the Memory Wall

insights.claim: TeRAM builds custom 3D SRAM memory chips specifically for frontier AI use cases, aiming to break down the 'Memory Wall' that the company believes is now constraining the continued scaling and adoption of frontier AI models.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific memory-technology bet (3D SRAM) as a proposed solution to the AI memory bottleneck, a space also being addressed by HBM and emerging DRAM approaches — relevant for tracking which memory architecture wins in AI accelerator design.
insights.quote: TeRAM builds custom 3D SRAM memory chips for frontier AI use.

insights.claim: Since the rollout of ChatGPT 3.5, AI models have increased 10X in size, and together with agentic workloads, this has stressed the memory subsystem, making AI both expensive and power-hungry.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A specific 10x model-size growth data point quantifies how fast memory demand has outpaced supply since late 2022/2023, supporting the broader thesis that memory (not just compute) is now the binding constraint on AI economics.
insights.quote: Since the rollout of ChapGPT 3.5, AI models have increased 10X in size and together with agentic workloads have stressed the memory subsystem to make AI both expensive and power hungry.

insights.claim: The Memory Wall arises because compute has scaled faster than memory can keep up on both bandwidth and density, and existing memory technologies are each hitting real physical limits as they are pushed harder, making those limits a genuine bottleneck for AI.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A clear articulation of the memory wall framework that investors can use to evaluate competing memory startups and incumbents (HBM, DRAM, SRAM) on whether they credibly address bandwidth vs. density limits.
insights.quote: The memory wall — compute has scaled faster than memory can keep up, on both bandwidth and density. Existing memory technologies each hit real physical limits as they’re pushed harder, and those limits are becoming a genuine bottleneck for AI.
insights.locator: What keeps your customers up at night?

insights.claim: TeRAM claims strength across all phases of AI development and deployment: scaling in capacity for frontier model training, scaling in bandwidth for the decode portion of inference, and — via its packaging advantages — potential extension to on-premise AI deployments and even edge devices such as AR/VR.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A broad applicability claim (training capacity, inference bandwidth, edge AR/VR) suggests TeRAM is targeting a wide total addressable market rather than a single niche, though this remains an unproven, self-reported claim to validate against design wins.
insights.locator: What application areas are your strongest?

insights.claim: TeRAM's business model is to sell memory chips customized for each customer's compute chip, a model the CEO explicitly likens to Broadcom's ASIC business, with hyperscalers or semiconductor companies providing specifications that TeRAM then designs customized chips against.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: The Broadcom-ASIC-business comparison signals a custom-silicon, design-win-driven revenue model rather than a merchant-memory-chip model — implying higher customer concentration risk but potentially higher margins and stickier relationships once a design win is secured.
insights.quote: So we are somewhat similar to Broadcom’s ASIC business. Customers such as hyperscalars or semiconductor companies provide us with specifications and we develop customized chips for their compute chips.
insights.locator: How do customers normally engage with your company?

insights.claim: TeRAM differentiates from existing DRAM and SRAM companies, who are also working on the Memory Wall problem, by claiming a unique approach that enables easier and more efficient packaging to deliver higher capacity and bandwidth at lower power consumption.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A direct competitive claim against incumbent DRAM/SRAM suppliers; as a self-reported differentiation without disclosed technical specifics, it should be weighted cautiously pending independent technical validation or customer disclosures.
insights.quote: However, we feel we have a completely unique approach to the problem, specifically how it results in a easier & more efficient packaging to deliver higher capacity, bandwidth at lower power consumption.
insights.locator: What does the competitive landscape look like

insights.claim: TeRAM sees a window of opportunity for a new memory solution because much work is still needed to extend the current DRAM and HBM roadmap to integrate with hybrid-bonding, while the industry waits for true 3D DRAM bit-cell mass production.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Frames TeRAM's product as a bridge technology filling a gap until 3D DRAM matures — useful for estimating TeRAM's realistic competitive window before incumbents' native 3D DRAM potentially obsoletes the need for a 3D SRAM alternative.
insights.quote: I think it’s important to note that much is needed to extend the current DRAM and HBM roadmap to integrate with hybrid-bonding while waiting for the true 3D DRAM bit-cell mass production. So there is a window of opportunity for a new way of solving the Memory Wall problem.
insights.locator: What new features/technology are you working on?

insights.claim: TeRAM spun out of Kilopass in 2018 following Kilopass's acquisition by Synopsys, raised its Seed funding rounds in 2026, and has raised $37 million total to validate its technology.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A concrete funding figure ($37M) and stage (Seed, closed 2026) for benchmarking TeRAM against other memory startups' capital intensity and maturity — notably still pre-revenue/pre-volume at this funding level for a hardware/memory startup.
insights.quote: We’ve raised $37M so far to validate our technology.
insights.locator: We spun out of Kilopass in 2018

insights.claim: TeRAM is privately held, headquartered in Silicon Valley, with development centers and a fabrication partner based in Asia.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Confirms TeRAM is fabless with an Asia-based fab partner, meaning its supply chain and manufacturing risk are tied to Asian foundry capacity rather than an in-house fab.

insights.claim: CEO Charlie Cheng has four decades of experience in microprocessor architecture and semiconductor memory, previously worked on multiple generations of Meta's MTIA AI accelerators beginning in 2019, and was CEO of memory IP company Kilopass where he secured SK hynix and Samsung as licensees before its acquisition by Synopsys.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A credibility signal for TeRAM: the CEO has direct AI-accelerator design experience (Meta MTIA) and a track record of licensing memory IP to top-tier memory makers (SK hynix, Samsung), which may aid TeRAM's ability to secure design wins or partnerships with major memory or AI compute companies.
insights.locator: Charlie Cheng is CEO of TeRAM
